name: Zoe Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day splits in two. Early on I'm outside with Graham, my husband: feeding the forty ewes, moving the pigs we fatten for the shop, checking the potatoes in the store. From nine I'm in the farm shop on the Hollow Road, which sells our own lamb, pork, potatoes and eggs, plus jams and cheese from other farms nearby. I like the mix, and I like the regulars, but the shop never quite switches off, even at night I'm thinking about the order for Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else keeps the place going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pam and Ruby work the shop part time, Pam's been with us nine years and knows every customer by name. Our son Owen helps on the farm two days a week and works at a call centre in town the rest. Our daughter Kate is a nurse up north, she comes back at lambing to help, mostly to tell me I'm doing it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a handy tool. I use one now and then to help write the shop's posts on social media, because I'm hopeless at it and Ruby's too busy. Nobody coming to buy a leg of lamb cares how I wrote the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means very little. If it helps me write the weekly email to customers in ten minutes instead of an hour, that's an hour back on a Sunday. The shop's about people, and the farm's about weather, neither of those changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it for the posts and the email, maybe try it for the staff rota, once I've seen how Mary at the garden centre gets on with hers. On the farm, the big job this year would be new guttering on the lambing shed, about two thousand. And I'd keep the shop's Christmas orders on paper, because that's how customers like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a better pencil, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait to see Mary's rota before trying it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a rota is people's lives. If I get the email wrong, someone gets a typo, but if I get the rota wrong, Pam misses her granddaughter's school play. Mary's got twelve staff, so if it works for her, it'll work for my three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said customers like Christmas orders on paper. How do you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I tried online orders three years ago and half of them rang me up anyway to check. They want to hear Pam say, yes, your turkey's down for the twenty-third. That phone call is part of what they're buying.

S0.say: It's a handy tool, and I use one now and then to write the shop's social media posts. Nobody buying a leg of lamb cares how I wrote the post.
S0.think: It means very little, apart from writing the weekly customer email in ten minutes instead of an hour. The shop is about people and the farm is about weather, and neither changes.
S0.do: Keeps using the assistant for posts and emails and considers it for the staff rota once she has seen it work at Mary's garden centre. Puts in new guttering on the lambing shed for about two thousand and keeps Christmas orders on paper.
S0.feel: Calm, seeing it as a better pencil.
S0.quote: If I get the rota wrong, Pam misses her granddaughter's school play.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is a steady adopter who tests tools on low-stakes jobs and waits for proof before trusting them with anything that affects people. She knows her customers well, including that the phone call is part of the product. Her farm shop is the heart of her identity more than the livestock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds manageable, and that the sensible thing is to train people as it goes. Some help for young people would make sense, but I wouldn't want the government paying for everything. I'd say it to the other shop owners at the market traders' meeting, and we'd probably agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's quite gentle. I'm fifty-eight, I'll be winding down as it spreads. Owen's the one I think about, because a call centre job is exactly the kind of beginner work that gets cut slowly, and he's only twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Owen about working more days on the farm and in the shop, maybe running the butchery counter, which Graham wants to step back from. That would mean paying him properly, maybe twelve thousand a year more than now, so we'd have to grow the shop to cover it. I'd look at opening on Sundays, which we've always resisted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy for Owen, but there's a hopeful bit too, that he might come home to the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Opening on Sundays. Why have you always resisted it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's our one day off, honestly, and Graham's chapel in the morning. But if it means Owen has a proper job here, I'd give up Sundays. Graham would grumble and then do it, that's how our marriage works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Owen say if you offered him the butchery counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes and then panic. He's good with customers from the call centre, better than me, actually, but he's never boned out a lamb. Graham would have to teach him, and Graham's not a patient teacher.

S1.say: It sounds manageable, and the sensible thing is to train people as it goes. Some help for young people makes sense, but I don't want the government paying for everything.
S1.think: It's quite gentle for me because I'll be winding down as it spreads. Owen's the one I think about, because his call centre job is the kind of beginner work that slowly disappears.
S1.do: Offers Owen more days on the farm and the butchery counter that Graham wants to give up, paying him about twelve thousand a year more. Opens the shop on Sundays to cover the cost.
S1.feel: A little uneasy for Owen, with a hopeful sense that he might come home to the business.
S1.quote: Graham would grumble and then do it, that's how our marriage works.
S1.fieldNote: She turns the threat to her son's job into a succession plan, with real costs attached like giving up Sundays. Her centrist view shows in wanting help for young people without the state paying for everything. The family dynamics come through warmly and precisely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a middle way: help people retrain, make sure firms pay their share, but don't panic and ban things. I'd say it in the shop, because everyone talks politics at the till, and I try not to take sides too loudly. It's bad for business to fall out with half your customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Owen's call centre job goes, full stop. And a lot of my regular customers are office workers in town, so if they lose pay, they stop buying the good sausages and start buying the cheap ones at the supermarket. The shop could lose a fifth of its takings without anything changing on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring Owen in full time on the shop and farm straight away, before he's laid off, so he isn't sitting at home feeling useless. I'd start a cheaper line, mince and sausage packs and a soup bag of our own vegetables, for people watching their money. And I'd cut my own drawings from the business for a year, Graham and I can live on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yes. Busy-anxious, though, the kind where you've got a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cutting your own drawings. What actually goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we'd planned to see Kate in the spring, and the new car. We've got about three months of costs saved, and I'd rather keep that untouched. The old car has done two hundred thousand kilometres, it can do a few more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who among your regulars would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a couple, the Hendersons, both at the council offices, they come every Saturday for a chicken and a chat. If they both lost their jobs, I'd notice, because they'd stop coming, and they'd be embarrassed. I'd probably put an extra something in the bag and say it was going out of date.

S2.say: We need a middle way: help people retrain and make firms pay their share, but don't panic and ban things. I try not to take sides loudly at the till, because it's bad for business to fall out with half your customers.
S2.think: I think Owen's call centre job goes, full stop. My regulars are office workers in town, so if their pay drops they switch to cheap supermarket sausages, and the shop could lose a fifth of its takings.
S2.do: Brings Owen into the business full time before he can be laid off and launches a cheaper range of mince, sausage packs and soup bags. Cuts her own drawings for a year by dropping a planned trip to see Kate and keeping the old car.
S2.feel: Anxious, but busy-anxious, the kind of worry that comes with a list.
S2.quote: I'd probably put an extra something in the bag and say it was going out of date.
S2.fieldNote: Her farm is exposed through the shop's customers rather than through its own work, which is a sharp insight. She moves quickly but within her means, protecting savings by cutting family spending. Her quiet kindness to struggling regulars is typical of how she sees the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there has to be a deal, and soon, where the people who've done very well share some of it, through taxes, but sensibly. I'd say the shouting on both sides makes it worse. In the shop I'd keep my head down and my prices fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's strange. House prices booming means we'd get new money moving into the villages, people from the city who can afford farm shop prices. But my old regulars would be losing jobs, so the shop would change, more posh cheese, fewer Saturday chickens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably follow the money a bit: stock more of the expensive lines, maybe start a café corner, because the newcomers would want that. But I'd keep the cheaper packs going for the regulars. Owen could run the café side, he's good with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Doing well while people you know are struggling doesn't sit right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help with any of that new business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the menus and the pricing, probably, once I'd seen it work for the café in the next village. I'd ask it to tell me what a coffee should cost here, then ask Ruby, who'd know better. It's a starting point, not the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said doing well doesn't sit right. What would you do about that feeling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the vicar about a food bank shelf in the shop, where people can leave things for others. We did that in the floods in 2015. It doesn't fix anything big, but it means the shop's still for everyone.

S3.say: There has to be a deal soon where the people who've done very well share some of it through sensible taxes. The shouting on both sides makes it worse, so I'd keep my head down and my prices fair.
S3.think: It's strange, because booming house prices bring new city money into the villages that can afford farm shop prices. But my old regulars would be losing jobs, so the shop would shift to posh cheese and fewer Saturday chickens.
S3.do: Stocks more expensive lines and opens a café corner run by Owen for the newcomers, while keeping the cheaper packs for regulars. Talks to the vicar about a food bank shelf in the shop, as they did in the 2015 floods.
S3.feel: Uneasy, because doing well while people she knows struggle doesn't sit right.
S3.quote: Doing well while people you know are struggling doesn't sit right.
S3.fieldNote: She is one of the few who might gain in this scenario, and she admits it while feeling uncomfortable about it. Her plans follow the money but keep space for old customers. She uses AI as a first guess and checks it against her staff, a steady habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow the robots down, or at least make sure people have time to adjust, maybe a few years' grace for small businesses. I'm not against them, I'd say, but you can't change everything at once. I'd say that to our MP, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the farm side would get harder, because big farms with robots would sell lamb and potatoes cheaper. But the shop might be the bit that survives. People don't drive six miles for a cheaper carrot. They come because Pam remembers their dog's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift the business more toward the shop and less toward the farm. Maybe cut the ewes to twenty, keep the pigs because they're for the shop, and buy in more from neighbours. I'd see how a robot did at the big farm over the hill before thinking of one, and I'd keep Pam and Ruby whatever happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed for the farm, calmer for the shop. It's an odd split.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep Pam and Ruby whatever happened. What if the numbers say otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd cut my own hours and Graham's before theirs. Pam's sixty-two, where else is she going to work? I'd rather have a smaller farm than a shop without Pam in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen about his future here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the shop is the future, not the sheep. Learn the people side, learn the buying, and let the robots do the boring bits if they ever come. He'll be fine if he keeps the customers.

S4.say: We need to slow the robots down and give small businesses a few years' grace to adjust. I'm not against them, but you can't change everything at once.
S4.think: The farm side would get harder because big farms with robots would sell cheaper. But the shop might survive, because people don't drive six miles for a cheaper carrot, they come because Pam remembers their dog's name.
S4.do: Shifts the business toward the shop by cutting the ewes to twenty and buying in more from neighbours. Watches a robot at the big farm over the hill before considering one, and keeps Pam and Ruby on by cutting her and Graham's hours first.
S4.feel: Close to alarmed for the farm but calmer about the shop, an odd split.
S4.quote: People don't drive six miles for a cheaper carrot. They come because Pam remembers their dog's name.
S4.fieldNote: Zoe sees the shop's human touch as the part of her business robots can't easily take. She is willing to shrink farming to protect it and her staff. Her steady approach shows again: watch a neighbour's robot before deciding anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, for the farm side. What would help is a slower start for small farms and some help to make farm shops and local selling easier, maybe grants for chillers and things. And keeping the town's jobs going, because the town is my customer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who aren't on the payroll. The farm shop is half a meeting place, people come for the chat as much as the sausages. People don't drive six miles for a cheaper carrot. They come because Pam remembers their dog's name.

headlineQuote: People don't drive six miles for a cheaper carrot. They come because Pam remembers their dog's name.
portrait: Zoe Abbott is a 58-year-old farmer who runs a small mixed farm with her husband Graham and a busy farm shop with two long-serving staff. She uses AI for small jobs like social media posts and waits to see tools work for neighbours before trusting them with anything that touches people. Across the scenarios she reads risk through her customers and her son's call centre job, bringing him into the business early and adding cheaper lines. When robots arrive, she would shrink the farm side and bet on the shop, keeping her staff even if it means cutting her own hours.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because big farms with robots would undercut her farm produce.
whatWouldHelp: A slower start for robots on small farms, grants to help farm shops and local selling, and keeping jobs in the nearby town.
